passage: June in Johannesburg meant frost on the car windows. Bao's mum drove him to school every morning with the heater on. One Tuesday, at a red light, Bao saw Lindiwe from his class walking along the road, her breath making clouds, her hands pulled into her sleeves. The school was still far. "Mum, why does Lindiwe walk?" "Her family doesn't have a car, love." "But it's so cold." "Yes." Bao pressed his hand against the warm vent and suddenly didn't like how warm it was. At school, Lindiwe arrived late, rubbing her fingers. Bao wanted to say sorry, but for what? That evening he asked, "Could we give her a lift?" His mum thought. "We could ask her family."

qa.q: What did Bao see on the car windows in June?
qa.a: Frost.

qa.q: What was Bao feeling when he pressed his hand against the warm vent?
qa.a: He felt guilty and uneasy, suddenly noticing his warmth while Lindiwe walked in the cold, and curious about why things were different.

qa.q: What is a respectful next step for Bao's idea of a lift?
qa.a: Asking Lindiwe's family first, as his mum suggested, so the offer respects them instead of assuming.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel arriving late and cold every day?
qa.a: She may feel tired and uncomfortable, and perhaps embarrassed to arrive late for reasons that aren't her fault.

grounding: Illustrates a child noticing a classmate walks far in the cold while he arrives by car, and starting to ask why.

passage: During the Diwali holidays, the school ran a study camp in the library. Urmila noticed that Vandana always came first and left last, even though the camp ended at five. "Why don't you go home to study?" Urmila asked one afternoon. Vandana shrugged. "Our house is one room. My cousins are visiting for Diwali. There's nowhere to sit." Urmila thought of her own desk, the lamp, the closed door. "Oh." A boy nearby said, "Urmila's got her own room, lucky." "It's not my fault," Urmila snapped, surprising herself. Later she felt bad about it. On the way out she asked the librarian, "Can the library stay open longer for people who need it?" The librarian said she would ask the principal.

qa.q: How many rooms is Vandana's house?
qa.a: One room.

qa.q: Why did Urmila snap "It's not my fault"?
qa.a: She felt defensive and a little guilty when the boy pointed out her own room, as if she were being blamed for her advantage.

qa.q: What was helpful about Urmila's question to the librarian?

qa.q: How might Vandana see Urmila's questions?
qa.a: Vandana may feel a bit exposed explaining her home, but also noticed and perhaps glad someone asked the librarian.

grounding: Shows a child realising a classmate has no quiet place to study, asking why and feeling defensive and guilty.

passage: When the results came out, I, Joseph, was second in the class. At lunch, Jasleen said, not unkindly, "Well, you've had maths tuition since Class 6. Some of us can't afford that." I felt like she'd slapped me. "I worked hard," I said, too loudly. "I studied every night." "I know," she said. "I didn't say you didn't." I sulked all afternoon. Later, at home, I watched my tutor arrive, and I thought about Jasleen studying alone. Both things were true. I did work hard. And I also had help she didn't. The second thing doesn't cancel the first. It took me a week to say that to her. She just nodded and said, "Thanks."

qa.q: What position did Joseph come in the class?
qa.a: Second in the class.

qa.q: Why did Joseph feel "slapped" by Jasleen's remark?
qa.a: Joseph felt attacked and defensive, as if she were saying the result wasn't earned at all.

qa.q: What helped Joseph understand Jasleen's point?
qa.a: Watching the tutor arrive and picturing Jasleen studying alone helped Joseph see that hard work and extra help can both be true.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have felt when Joseph finally spoke to her?
qa.a: Jasleen likely felt understood and respected, which is why she simply said "Thanks."

grounding: Shows a teenager told they had it easier reacting defensively with "I worked hard" before seeing both things are true.

passage: Robotics club note, Friday. Tejas and Manjula argued today after I announced the summer lab placements. Manjula said, "Of course Tejas got it, his father knows the lab director." Tejas went red and said, "I built that robot arm myself! I worked on it for months!" Both were right, and neither could hear the other. I asked them to sit with me after the session. I told Tejas his effort was real, and that the phone call from his father also helped him get noticed. I told Manjula her frustration made sense. Tejas was quiet for a long while. What I did next: I've asked the lab to add an open application round next year, so every club member has the same way in.

passage:
Wednesday night
In the inter-school debate today, Arnab lost to me and then said in the corridor, "Easy for you. Your school's English medium. You've been debating since you were small." I said, "Excuse me, I practised every single day for three weeks." And I walked off. I was so angry I couldn't eat dinner. How dare he? But now, lying here, I keep thinking about his speech. His arguments were actually good. He just kept stopping to find words. I never have to do that. I did practise every day. That's true. It's also true I had a head start he didn't. I hate that both are true. Maybe tomorrow I'll tell him his rebuttal on point two was the best one there.

passage:
Thursday
I've been thinking about English. I went to a convent school and my English came free, really. I didn't earn it; I just grew up in it. At work that means managers hear me first. Today Nilesh presented his plan, and it was better than mine, but he kept stumbling on words, and the room drifted. Afterwards I didn't say "I feel so bad". That helps nobody. I asked him if he wanted to practise the next one together. He said yes. I also forwarded him the leadership course that nobody told him about. passage: Nirmala, beta, come see this old box. You're upset because Rhea got more medals than you? Let me tell you about winter sports day when I was nine. I, your Pradeep Dadu, won one bronze for the sack race. I was so proud, I ran all the way home. Then I saw my neighbour's son with three golds on his coat. Suddenly my bronze looked like a bottle cap. I threw it in this very box and didn't look at it for years. Silly boy. That bronze was for my best race ever. Only later did I understand that measuring myself against him taught me where I stood, but it shouldn't have told me what I was worth.

passage: The power went out just as Class 5's term results were being read during the Holi week assembly, so the teacher shouted the marks in the dim hall. Disha strained to hear. On the way back to class, she asked everyone their marks, one by one, keeping a list in her head. Above her: four. Below her: many. She felt a little better, then worse again. At home, Papa asked about the result. "I'm fifth," she said. "No, what did you get?" "Eighty-eight." "That's your best ever." Disha blinked. She hadn't thought of it that way at all.

passage:

You asked why I've been quiet on calls. It's silly. Every night I scroll before sleeping and everyone's life looks amazing. Someone's at a science camp, someone got into a dance academy, someone's holiday photos are like a film. Then I look at my room with the fan that squeaks, and I feel so boring. Like I'm behind in a race nobody told me had started. Last Sunday I saw a girl from my class posting a perfect smiling photo. That same day she'd told me at tuition she was dreading her exam. So maybe I'm only seeing the best seconds of their weeks. I'm going to try keeping my phone outside my room this week. Tell me how your ordinary days go?

passage: Counsellor's note, Wednesday. Vidya came in today, a little embarrassed. Her closest friend Sonali had been promoted to team lead, the role they had both hoped for. What we agreed: she would call Sonali, admit that she was a little jealous and also truly proud, and suggest a celebration dinner. She texted me later that Sonali laughed and said, "I'd have felt the same."

passage:
Saturday night
Sahil got engaged today. My oldest friend. We did everything together since Class 1. I found out on the group chat, a photo of a ring, fifty heart replies. I typed "so happy for you!!" and meant it. Then I sat on the balcony for an hour feeling like I'd been left behind at a bus stop. Everyone's moving forward and I'm still here, same job, same flat. I don't even want to get married right now! So why does it sting? Maybe because it means things will change between us. I'm going to call Sahil tomorrow and say it straight: I'm thrilled and a bit sad I'm losing my partner-in-crime. Then I'll help plan the sangeet.
Simran

passage: Deepika's bakery in the kasba was one room with a single oven. Every night she used to scroll through Harsha's bakery page from the city, with its glass counter and hundred-comment posts, and go to bed feeling like a failure. In March, she muted it. Then she opened the notebook where she had written last year's numbers of orders by hand. Last April: ten cakes a week. This April: twenty-six. She sat back in her plastic chair and smiled. She kept following two other small-town bakers who shared recipes and honest mistakes. One of them taught her a trick for the humid monsoon dough. Harsha's page was still there if she wanted it. Mostly, she didn't.

qa.q: How many cakes a week did Deepika make last April?
qa.a: Ten cakes a week.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she compared this April with last April?

qa.a: She follows two small-town bakers who share recipes and honest mistakes, learning from them without feeling crushed.

qa.a: It left her feeling like a failure every night, even though her bakery was growing.

grounding: Shows a young professional muting a page that leaves her low, measuring against her past year, and learning from a few peers.

passage: Vera had been a junior architect in Cape Town for a year when she caught herself refreshing a classmate's feed again. Another award. Another glossy building. She put the phone down and opened last year's sketchbook instead. Her first drawings were stiff, the stairs wrong. Now her senior asked her to check other people's stairs. She laughed out loud. That evening she muted three accounts that always left her flat. She kept Lindiwe's, a friend two years ahead of her who posted drafts and failures along with finished work. She messaged her: "Coffee? I want to ask how you learnt site meetings." Lindiwe sent back a thumbs up. Vera wrote in her diary: compare with January Vera, not with everyone.

passage: In the physiotherapy department of the city hospital, the junior staff kept a whiteboard of who had handled the most patients. Ojas was always near the bottom, and it gnawed at him. passage: Before: In the winter term, Jatin's teacher said, "Jatin, lazy again?" when he forgot his homework. The class laughed. By January, everyone called him Lazy Jatin. He stopped raising his hand. Why try? During: In February, a new teacher, Miss Elizabeth, came. On her second day, she watched him fix the broken window latch. "You're a careful thinker, Jatin. Can you help with the science model?" Jatin blinked. After: Two weeks later, Jatin stayed back after class to finish the model's wiring. Nobody called him lazy while he did it. Miss Elizabeth kept giving him harder jobs, and he kept taking them.

grounding: Illustrates a child called lazy who stops trying, then takes on harder work when a teacher sees him as capable.

passage: Gurpreet, puttar, sit. You're sad because your cousin calls you slow? Listen to your Vikas Dadu. When I was ten, every Baisakhi at the fair, my uncles would laugh, "This one's a slow bullock, always last." After a while I believed them. At school I didn't even try the sums; why try if you're slow? Then a new master came. He saw me measure the wheat sacks for my father without a mistake. "Vikas, you have a sharp head. Try this." He gave me the hardest sum on the board. I got it on the third try. After that I wanted the hard ones. Words people say about you can become a coat you wear, puttar. You can take it off.

qa.q: What did Vikas's uncles call him at the Baisakhi fair?
qa.a: "A slow bullock, always last."

qa.q: How did the label make young Vikas feel?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and small, coming to believe he was slow and stopping even trying the sums.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Vikas?
qa.a: The new master saw him measure the wheat sacks without a mistake, called him sharp and gave him the hardest sum, which he solved.

qa.q: How might the new master have felt watching Vikas solve the sum?
qa.a: He probably felt pleased and proud, seeing his belief in Vikas confirmed.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how, as a boy, being called slow made him try less and being called sharp made him take on hard tasks.

passage: The wedding house was full of noise and May heat, and the aunties kept the children busy with puzzles. "Shalini, you're the clever one, you do the big one," said Bua, handing her a five-hundred-piece jungle puzzle. "Disha, you're a bit slow, take this small one." Disha looked at her puzzle of a cat, only forty pieces. Shalini sat down happily with the jungle, frowning in concentration. Disha fitted a few cat pieces, then pushed the rest aside and wandered off to watch the dhol players. "See, she never finishes," Bua said. Nobody noticed that Disha had been the one who finished the hardest crossword at breakfast. She had just stopped trying things people said were too hard for her.

qa.q: How many pieces did the cat puzzle have?
qa.a: Only forty pieces.

qa.q: Why did Disha push the cat puzzle aside?
qa.a: She felt discouraged and hurt at being called slow, so she stopped trying and wandered off.

qa.q: What could Bua do differently next time?
qa.a: She could let both girls choose their puzzle and avoid labels like "clever" or "slow".

qa.a: Shalini feels confident enough to take on the big puzzle, showing how the label pushes her to try hard tasks.

grounding: Illustrates how being called slow makes a child try less while a child called clever takes on hard tasks.
